topics.topic: correcting the unit 2 dictation drills at the board - drill 5 walked through together word by word, then drills 4 and 11 with students called up one at a time to write while she wrote the correct version alongside. Every word was analysed the same way: hear which letters are in it, then decide which of the four forms each letter takes

the short vowels (tashkeel) - fatha, damma, kasra and sukun: the shape of each mark, whether it sits above or below the letter, the sound it gives, and then every taught letter (alif, baa, taa, thaa, waaw, yaa) drilled through all four. Included the word-initial hamza rule and why sukun is normally not written at the end of a word

speaking practice with the unit 2 question words - ma ismuka/ismuki, min ayna anta/anti, hal, ayy madiina, ma ism abuka/abuki - asked around the room with students answering and being corrected. She had promised on Monday that Thursday would be the first speaking class and it was

yaa, the third and last long vowel - two dots or a dash, the curve that dips BELOW the line (unlike the tooth of baa/taa/thaa, which sits on it), all four positional forms, its double life as vowel (ii) and consonant (y), and the possessive suffix -ii built onto ab to give abii

announcements.text: Homework is due tomorrow, Friday 9/4. She said it twice, once mid-class and once in the closing seconds. Critically, she also said the work is now nearly done for them: drills 4, 5 and 11 were corrected on the board today, so 'you just need to take picture and upload it to Canvas'. This is a photograph-and-submit job, not a work-it-out job.

Drill 13 was NOT corrected today - she ran out of time and said it will be done Tuesday. She told the class to write it out at home first, connecting the letters into words as the book's example shows, and to pronounce each syllable out loud while writing, going back to the start of the word after each syllable the way Arab children learn to read.

The homework heading requirement was repeated as a standing rule: label every submission with the drill number, the homework number and the unit number. This is the second class in a row she has said it.

Sukun is not required on written homework. Asked directly whether the class should be writing it, she said 'I will not deduct whether you write it or you don't write it.' She will still mark it and talk about it in class. She also said casual written Arabic carries no tashkeel at all - not in newspapers, not in film subtitles - and that she will teach them step by step how to read without it.

Study advice, given unprompted and with some force: get into a group chat, reserve a room in the library, do the homework together and practise speaking with each other. She said group study is the single best way to prepare for exams in a language course. She closed the class with 'if you don't speak, you're not doing well for your Arabic.'

She offered to demonstrate a free Arabic Bible program with full tashkeel, but cannot install it on her Liberty laptop, so she will bring her personal laptop another day. She also pointed at Logos and at hard copies on Amazon.
She checked at the end of class that everyone now has the physical textbook.

position.next: unit 2 drill 13, corrected Tuesday; the consonant values of waaw and yaa come later, in unit 3
position.said: 'Today, the plan, I'm going to teach you one more letter, which is the third vowel. And we're going to write some of the drills... we did #2. We're going to do 4, 5, 11, and 13. And I have also to teach you today the short vowels'... 'Now, Drill 13, I will not correct it today, maybe we'll do it Tuesday'... 'so we'll do drill 13 on the, we'll do it on Tuesday'... 'I think chapter 3, where we teach you how to read the [yaa] as a consonant, not as a vowel.' Everything today was inside unit 2; unit 3 was named only as where consonantal waaw and yaa arrive.

commitments.title: Write out unit 2 drill 13 before Tuesday's class - connect the letters into words per the book's example, saying each syllable aloud as you write; she corrects it in class

off_slide: Opened in prayer, asking for health, immunity and care over hygiene on campus after a student mentioned six people were already out sick in week two

The two-stage dictation method restated as the core skill: first hear which letters are in the word, then decide which of the four forms each takes based on whether the previous letter connects leftward. She ran every drill word through it in that order

Stacked letters: a student wrote baa sitting on top of yaa rather than beside it, and she stopped to say both are correct, that some fonts stack, and that stacking becomes common with letters yet to come
Accent digression when a student heard the vowel in baab as closer to English 'e' - she attributed it to the recording's Egyptian speaker and said alif is A, with accents pulling it around

Page 33 of the book: an Arabic shop sign that is really an English clothing brand written in Arabic letters. She used it to show that names get Arabicized and Arabic names get Englishized, and repeated Monday's suggestion to type a word like baab in a Word document and cycle the fonts to see how far the shapes move

Page 5 of the book: the Quran and the Arabic Bible printed side by side, to show how much heavier the Quran's diacritics are - including an extra-long fatha she said exists only in Quranic text, for recitation

The Quran digression that came out of it, cut short with 'that's for another day': tajwid as an entire science of how to recite, Uthman's standardization of the text and what happened to the other copies, early manuscripts differing from modern printed ones, and Syriac vocabulary in the Quran. She mentioned she also teaches an intro to Islam course. Parker asked whether the heavy diacritics exist so the recitation cannot be misread, and she confirmed that is the reason
She told the class Arabic teaching does not traditionally split the alphabet into vowels and consonants, and that she uses the distinction anyway because it helps English speakers

The word-initial hamza rule, taught as a listening test: if a word starts with a glottal stop it takes hamza on the alif - written above for fatha and damma, below for kasra - the one exception being the definite article al-, which takes no hamza
Register revisited: hadratuka/hadratuki is optional extra politeness, not a rule for addressing a professor, and using anta/anti is not offensive

Vocabulary taught past its gloss again: tuut (berries) reconfirmed as a required word, baab as door, taabuut which she glossed as casket, abii as my father, and the Shami variant abuuki flagged as regional but fine
Corrected a student who started a question with both hal and ayna - the two cannot stack, a question starts with one or the other
Answered her own speaking prompts on the record: she is from Syria, from the city of Damascus, and lives in Lynchburg; her father's name is Elias, which she glossed as Elijah
Parker was called on twice by name in the speaking round and got it right both times, and he asked how to say goodbye when someone is leaving (ma'a salaama)
terms: fatha - short a, written above the letter
damma - short u, written above the letter, shaped like a small waaw
kasra - short i, written below the letter
sukun - no vowel, a small circle above the letter
ism / ismii / ismuka / ismuki - name / my name / your name
bil-arabi / bil-inglizi - in Arabic / in English
tajwid - the science of Quranic recitation

quotes.text: I made it easy for you guys. Now you have so many drills already completed for you. So you just need to take picture and upload it to Canvas.
Enjoy your weekend. I'll see you Tuesday. You have homework due tomorrow. Okay, so make sure you submit on time.
Please, if you don't speak, you're not doing well for your Arabic. Take advantage that you are in a class.

notes: ANKI DECK GATE MOVES. One new letter today, yaa, plus all four tashkeel marks (fatha, damma, kasra, sukun). The taught letter set is now alif, baa, taa, thaa, waaw, yaa - six letters, which is every letter needed for the unit 2 drills - and the short vowels are now fair game as card material. The deck has been held to the taught set on purpose; this is the biggest opening it has had.

Friday's homework is ALREADY on the due list twice (both rows dated 2026-09-04, from the 9/1 record and from due-watch). No commitment is emitted for it here, because a third near-identical row would be noise on a page where the item is due today anyway. What today ADDS is the effort estimate: drills 4, 5 and 11 were corrected on the board, so the remaining work is photographing and uploading, not solving.

Drill 13 is the one genuine ambiguity. She deferred correcting it to Tuesday, but Homework 2 is due Friday - so either drill 13 is not part of Homework 2, or it is being submitted uncorrected. She did not say which. The commitment above is worded as PREP for Tuesday rather than as a graded submission, which is safe under either reading; do not treat it as a second Canvas upload without checking Lingco or Canvas.

Nearly half the class - about 31 of 75 minutes - was students at the board writing dictation words while she corrected them. That is the pace signal: the drills are the course right now, not the vocabulary.

Page 33 and page 5 were LOOKED AT in class, not assigned. assigned_reading is deliberately empty; no reading and no page range was assigned. Both numbers are printed page labels as she spoke them, not physical PDF pages.

Her handwriting rules for yaa are worth a card each because they are the discriminators: the yaa tail is CURVY and dips below the line, where the tooth of baa/taa/thaa is straight and sits on it; and yaa in initial and medial position is identical to baa except for the two dots being below rather than above.
No Arabic script appears anywhere in this file. Teams has no Arabic, so everything here is transliteration and must be checked against her slides or the book before a card is made.

Transcript quality on the material that matters is poor, as usual. Letter and mark names came through as: yaa = 'Yell', 'yeah', 'year'; alif = 'LF', 'left', 'Alex', 'a left'; baa = 'bar', 'Bob', 'bow', 'va'; taa = 'tab', 'top'; thaa = 'that', 'th'; waaw = 'wall', 'wow', 'well'; fatha = 'fat ha', 'fat hat', '5th half', 'Fadha'; damma = 'dongma', 'Dagma', 'dog mom', 'dumb bump'; kasra = 'Kesra', 'Kesa', 'crossword', 'Sarah'; sukun = 'succon', 'suku', 'skill', 'sheep', 'the ski'; tashkeel = 'tashki', 'the scheme', 'the skill', 'Tashkil'; tajwid = 'the Jude'; hamza = 'hands up', 'hands at', 'hamsa'; Lingco = 'Lingo'; ismuki = 'smokey'; madiina = 'Medina'. Nothing above was reconstructed from a single garbled hit alone.

One line is transcribed as her saying the Quran evidence point in a way that reverses itself ('we use this as evidence that the Quran was altered, that otherwise it was altered'). The audio is unreliable exactly there and she moved on immediately, so no position is attributed to her beyond the factual points she made about Uthman's standardization and manuscript variation.
